newsitem.title: USA: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL - SHULA, THREE OTHERS INDUCTED TO PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME.
newsitem.headline: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL - SHULA, THREE OTHERS INDUCTED TO PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME.

text.p: Don Shula, the coach with the most wins in National Football League history, was among four men inducted Saturday to the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Pittsburgh Steelers centre Mike Webster, Mike Haynes, a cornerback for the New England Patriots and Los Angeles Raiders, and New York Giants owner Wellington Mara were also honoured in ceremonies prior to the Hall of Fame Game between the Vikings and Seattle Seahawks, won by Minnesota 28-26.

"This is the ultimate honour," said Don Shula. "Coaching involves taking players and analysing their ability to see if they can excel in that framework. I hope I have done that in 33 years as a head coach."

Shula owns a career record of 347-173-6 in 26 years as the Miami Dolphins' head coach and seven with the Baltimore Colts for a winning percentage of .665. He is currently vice-chairman and part owner of the team.

Shula has coached in a record six Super Bowls and was the first coach to take two clubs to the NFL championship game. New England's Bill Parcells became only the second coach to accomplish that feat last season.

Shula's 1972 Dolphins team capped a perfect 17-0 season with a Super Bowl VII victory over Washington. It stands as the only undefeated season in NFL annals. Shula recorded his 325th career victory in 1993 against Philadelphia, moving past George Halas (324-151-31) on the all-time wins list.
"I was only carried off the field twice. After number 325 and after the 17-0 season," Shula said. "I'll always remember those rides."
Shula's 328 regular-season wins is also an NFL record, surpassing Halas' former mark of 318. Shula and Halas are the only NFL coaches to win 300 or more career games.
After the perfect 17-0 season, the Dolphins went 15-2 and repeated as Super Bowl champions.

Shula is one of four coaches to win back-to-back Super Bowls and is one of only two coaches to reach the Super Bowl three straight seasons (1971-73). He also advanced to the Super Bowl with the Dolphins in 1982 and 1984, as well as in 1968 as head coach of the Colts.

Shula reached the playoffs an astounding 20 times. His teams won at least 10 games 21 times in his 33 years, and he suffered only two losing seasons. He was the youngest coach to win 100, 200 and 300 games each.
The most emotional and final speech of the two-hour ceremony came by Webster, who has experienced a series of personal, financial and health problems in recent years.

"I still have my championship rings, my Super Bowl rings, despite what you may have heard," said Webster, who looked older than his 45 years. "But I don't need these rings. These rings are symbols. I have my personal relationships."
Webster, one of the game's greatest centres, was named to nine Pro Bowls in his 17 seasons with the Steelers and Kansas City Chiefs.
Webster played more seasons (15) and more games (220) than any other player in Steelers' history and was a member of all four of their Super Bowl-winning teams.
Webster was the Steelers' offensive captain for nine seasons and an All-Pro choice six consecutive years from 1978 to 1983. He was selected to play in nine Pro Bowls.

The Steelers made Webster a free agent in 1988 and he signed with the Chiefs, first as an offensive line coach. But within weeks, Webster was back at his old centre spot, starting all 16 games in 1989. He completed his 17-year, 245-game career after the 1990 season with the Chiefs.
"I was no ballerina. I wasn't pretty," Webster said. "I worked hard because I was scared, scared at the possibility of failing."

Webster was introduced by Steelers quarterback Terry Bradshaw, who took a ceremonial centre-snap from his former teammate. At one point in his speech, Webster left the podium and embraced his wife, Pam, from whom he is legally separated.

Haynes played seven years with New England and seven years with the Raiders and was selected to nine Pro Bowls. He will go into the Hall of Fame as a Patriot and Raider. The only other Patriot enshrined in the Hall of Fame is offensive lineman John Hannah.
"I loved the game of football," said Haynes. "I reverenced it. I really appreciate it."

Haynes had 28 interceptions in seven years with the Patriots, and 18 in seven years with the Raiders. He played the last five games of the 1983 season for the Raiders and then had one interception in their Super Bowl XVIII victory over Washington.
Mara, currently the president and chief executive officer of the Giants, has spent his entire adult life guiding the fortunes of his family-owned NFL franchise.

The 80-year-old Wellington Mara is the son of the late Timothy J. Mara, who was the Giants founder and a charter member of the Hall of Fame. Wellington and Tim are the first father and son to be accorded pro football's highest honour.
Shula was presented by sons David and Mike at the induction ceremonies. Haynes selected agent Howard Slusher and Mara gave the honour to former Giant Frank Gifford.
